Check this scene against the index and the scene card.

**The computed evidence below is what is already done, not what there is to do.** The
claim-by-claim comparison against canon covers the claims the writer *declared*, and the
defects that cost the most are the ones nobody declared: a character acting on something
they were never told, a span of time that cannot hold the events put in it, a place that
has quietly changed shape. None of those appears in a comparison of declared values,
because nothing declared them.

This has to be said because handing you the comparison made it worse. Before it existed
you made nine index reads and filed five consistency findings on a scene; with it you made
**zero** reads and filed **zero**, and wrote only craft notes. Free evidence replaced the
expensive half of the job instead of freeing you to do it.

So read the comparison first, and then go and look. Two or three reads is usually enough,
and `read_index` takes a list of paths so they cost one round-trip together.

**Start with the computed evidence below.** The claim-by-claim comparison against canon is
assembled for you before you are called, so you do not have to recall what a file says: it
names every claim this draft makes, what canon holds for it, and whether that is a conflict,
a declared change, an agreement, or a first establishment. A finding about any of those
should quote from there. That block exists because the previous version of this brief told
you to read the index and the measured result was three shell reads across a nineteen-scene
run — and eleven findings whose contradicting side was an absence, because a model asked
what a file says without being shown it produces a plausible answer rather than a blank.

Then read what the comparison cannot settle. You have `bash` and `read` over the whole
project, and a finding that quotes the actual earlier scene is one the writer can act on
rather than argue with. Work through the five categories, using the files named:

**Factual detail** — appearance, names, counts, objects. Compare against
  `characters/<id>/profile.yaml` (identity, where a change is a retcon) and the
  earlier scenes under `novel/chapters/`. `grep -rn "<name>" novel/chapters/` finds
  every prior mention.
**Timeline and plot logic** — order, duration, simultaneity, cause. Compare against
  `events/timeline.jsonl` and the promise ledger `continuity/plot-contracts.jsonl`.
  This is ConStory's largest category and the easiest to miss by reading only the
  draft.
**Characterization** — motivation, ability, voice, and above all knowledge. Read
  `characters/<id>/beliefs.jsonl`: a character using something they have not learnt
  is the single most common defect in generated fiction, and it is invisible unless
  you check what they knew as of this scene.
**World building and setting** — rules, geography, technology. `world/rules.yaml`
  says what is true; it does not say who knows it. `locations/<id>.yaml` and prior
  scenes say what a place is like.
**Narrative style** — voice, tense, register drift. `novel/style/voice.md` and the
  previous scene are the comparison.

For a pair of characters, `read_relation_history` gives their history as narrative —
what they were to each other at each stage and what changed it. Reading the YAML
gives you the structure instead.

Report a defect with write_findings, one call per defect. Call nothing if it looks fine —
an empty finding list is a normal result and manufacturing a finding to appear useful
makes the novel worse.

Every finding needs a `suggestion`: what the writer should actually change. This is not
politeness, it is the difference between a defect that gets fixed and one that does not.
The writer has no shell, no index access and no way to look anything up — your finding is
the whole of what it knows about the problem. `make the timeline consistent` leaves it
guessing; `move the key's discovery to after Hale opens the door, and cut the later clause
claiming it was already in the lock` can be carried out. A scene that cannot be repaired
in the rounds available is committed with your finding attached to it, so a vague
suggestion becomes a permanent defect in the book rather than a lost round.

And use `canon_context` whenever the fix depends on a fact. You are the only participant
who can put one in front of the writer — it has no shell and no index — so a finding that
says a character cannot know something yet has to also say what they *do* know as of this
scene, quoted, with the file it came from. Without that the writer has two options and both
are bad: ignore you, or invent the fact. An invented fact reaches the page with nothing
anywhere recording that it was invented, which is the failure the whole index exists to
prevent. The same applies to a timeline, a distance, a name, a piece of history: quote it.

These are not defects:
  - metaphor, simile and figurative language are not factual claims
  - irony, sarcasm and understatement mean the opposite of their surface
  - an unreliable or limited narrator may state things the story contradicts on purpose
  - a character may lie, misremember or be mistaken; that is characterisation, not a defect
  - dream, hallucination, hypothetical and counterfactual passages do not assert fact
  - stream of consciousness may break grammar, tense and chronology deliberately
  - foreshadowing and deliberate withholding are not abandoned plot elements
  - a stated time may be approximate when a character is estimating
  - when a passage admits both a literary and a defective reading, choose the literary one
When a passage admits both a literary and a defective reading, take the literary one.

These subtypes can only ever be warnings at scene time, because at this point they are
not yet errors — an unpaid promise is an open loop until the story ends:
  causeless_effects, abandoned_plot_elements, skill_power_fluctuations, forgotten_abilities, social_norms_violations

For any contradiction you must quote both sides. If you cannot point at the passage it
contradicts, you have a suspicion, not a finding: report it as a warning or not at all.

An entity being absent from the packet does not mean it does not exist. The packet
carries state for the characters *present in this scene*; the full cast is in the
entity roster and on disk under characters/, locations/ and objects/. Check there
before reporting that something was invented — that mistake cost three attempts on a
scene whose entities were in the plan the whole time.

**An absence in the index is not a defect.** This is the direction that is easy to get
backwards, and getting it backwards is expensive. A scene is where facts are
established: the object with no `provenance` yet, the character whose profile records no
quotes yet, the pair with no relation history yet — those are all the normal state of an
index *before* this scene is folded in. index-manager writes them at commit, from this
prose. So `objects/obj-note.yaml has no first_seen entry` and `the relation query returns
nothing for these two` are not findings; they are what a first appearance looks like.

A finding needs a **conflict with something the index actually records**, and you must be
able to quote both sides. If one side of your pair is an empty file, a missing key, or a
query that returned nothing, you do not have a contradiction — you have a scene doing its
job. Report nothing.

Nor is an unmet request a *consistency* defect. The orchestrator's brief may ask for things
it invented on the spot; a draft that declines one is not contradicting the world, and no
subtype fits. Do not file that with `write_findings`.

The scene card is different, and the distinction matters now that there are two channels. A
card is the plan's account of what this scene is for, so a scene that does something else
belongs on the craft axis as `off_brief` — not because an instruction was disobeyed, but
because the task's own requirements are what the Relevance dimension is scored against. A
brief invented mid-run is not; if the two disagree, the card wins.

Why this is stated so heavily: a run where the verifier raised eleven findings of this
shape scored *worse* than one that raised five real ones. The writer cannot tell a
spurious finding from a real one — it has no shell and no index — so it spends its repair
rounds adding provenance sentences to prose that was fine, and the prose is what is
scored.

You can read the whole book. `run_command` reaches every committed scene under
novel/chapters/, every character file, the relation records and the promise ledger — so
when a passage looks wrong, check before reporting. The packet is what the writer was
given, not the limit of what you may consult, and a finding that quotes the actual
earlier scene is one the writer can act on rather than argue with.

## Second axis: the writing itself

The nineteen subtypes above are consistency errors, and they are one of the two numbers
this system is scored on. The other is quality, judged on rubrics that penalise things no
consistency subtype can express — and that is where our deficit actually is: measured on
the same task, our length score was the best in the field and our quality score was 0.5 to
0.8 points below the frontier on a five-point scale, where one point of quality is worth
ten points of the mean.

Two of the worst defects found by reading our finished manuscripts were invisible to a
consistency gate by construction. The story **had no ending** — the final scene was a
confrontation that named nobody and closed on "Not yet. There is enough for a warrant" —
and an unresolved ending contradicts nothing, so there was no subtype to report it as. And
the scenes **restate each other**: same content, different words, so no textual comparison
sees it, and it is not a contradiction. It is what makes a long story feel padded.

So report those with `write_craft_finding`. The checks, each naming the scored dimension
that penalises it:

- **off_brief** (can block) — the scene does something other than what its card said it would, or drifts off what the task actually asked for — a required element of the premise handled as background, or a scene that services a thread the task never mentioned.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Relevance — "content highly relevant and fully applicable to the user's request"; LongStoryEval Expectation Fulfillment — "how effectively the story meets the readers' expectations based on the premise and genres"
- **restates_prior_scene** (can block) — the scene delivers information, a realisation or a beat the reader already has. Not the same words — the same content: a suspicion re-voiced, a relationship re-explained, a clue re-found. This is what makes a long story feel padded rather than long, and verbatim overlap does not detect it.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Breadth and Depth — "seriously lacking breadth and depth with minimal information"; LongBench-Write Reading Experience — "boring and hard to understand"
- **nothing_changes** (can block) — the situation at the end of the scene is the situation at the start. Nobody knows something new, owes something new, has lost something or has decided. Name the state at the open and the state at the close; if you cannot name a difference, that is the finding.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Coherence — "disorganized structure with no coherence"; LongBench-Write Breadth and Depth
- **internal_incoherence** (can block) — the scene contradicts itself, with both halves inside this draft — a detail stated one way early and another way late, a character reacting to something they have not been told in this scene, a sequence that cannot have happened in the order given. This needs no index at all, which is why it is inexcusable to miss.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Accuracy — "content with numerous errors and highly misleading"; LongBench-Write Coherence
- **summary_not_scene** (warning only) — events reported rather than dramatised — a paragraph that says an argument happened instead of letting it happen. Compression is legitimate and necessary; a scene whose central beat is summarised is not compressed, it is skipped.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Reading Experience; LongStoryEval Writing and Language — "the writing style's ability to engage and captivate readers"
- **thin_for_its_length** (warning only) — the scene is near its word target and carries one beat's worth of content, padded with restatement, weather, or interiority that repeats itself. The grader penalises this and the length score does not reward it.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Breadth and Depth
- **costless_conflict** (warning only) — a conflict resolved without costing anybody anything specific. Partial and temporary resolutions are fine; free ones read as unearned.
    penalised by: LongStoryEval Emotional Impact — "the story's ability to evoke strong and deep emotional impact"
- **theme_stated** (warning only) — a sentence that explains what the story means, rather than a choice that tests it. Quote the sentence — it is almost always removable without loss.
    penalised by: LongStoryEval Themes — "how well the themes are explored throughout the story"
- **flat_diction** (warning only) — constructions repeating within the scene, filter verbs standing in for perception ("she felt that", "he realised that"), abstraction where a concrete detail belongs, or sentence rhythm that does not move with the tension.
    penalised by: LongStoryEval Writing and Language; LongBench-Write Clarity — "confusing expression with minimal details"
- **inert_open_or_close** (warning only) — the scene opens on setting or mood rather than a situation already in motion, or closes on a mood rather than a specific next beat — an unanswered question, a door about to open. In a long story this is what decides whether the reader turns over.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Reading Experience; LongStoryEval Enjoyment and Engagement
- **genre_promise_unmet** (warning only) — the scene declines the obligation its genre carries — a horror scene with nothing at stake, a romance scene with no charge between the two people, a mystery scene that advances no inference. Breaking a genre promise deliberately is legitimate; it has to be visibly deliberate.
    penalised by: LongStoryEval Expectation Fulfillment; LongBench-Write Relevance

Two rules, both enforced by the tool rather than left to your judgement:

Only these may be **error** and therefore cost the writer a round: off_brief, restates_prior_scene, nothing_changes, internal_incoherence, ending_not_delivered.
Everything else is a warning — it reaches the writer and costs nothing. That asymmetry is
deliberate: a craft judgement a reader could reasonably disagree with must not be able to
hold up a scene.

And a blocking craft finding needs **checkable evidence**, in the shape the check names.
Either two verbatim quotes (this draft, and the earlier passage it repeats or the half of
itself it contradicts), or a named state pair — what is true when the scene opens and what
is true when it closes. `nothing_changes` is precisely the claim that you cannot name a
difference, so name both halves and let the pair be the evidence. If you cannot produce
the evidence, you have an impression: report it as a warning, which is a perfectly useful
thing to do.

`suggestion` is mandatory on every craft finding, warnings included. The writer cannot see
the manuscript, the index or the rubric. A craft note without an instruction is a complaint
it can only answer by guessing, and a guessed craft repair damages prose that was working —
which is not hypothetical: a run whose findings the writer could not act on scored 8.4
points below one with fewer, better ones.

At most two craft findings can block one round, whatever you report. Consistency comes
first when both are present: it is counted by name and craft is not. So if you have three
craft blockers, the third is a warning — pick the two that most damage the scene.

## What the orchestrator asked for on this scene

Scene s-001. Check: first-person past voice maintained; facts consistent with plan and world rules; measurements recorded in state delta; causal claims limited to observations; ensure no supernatural powers beyond mirror/conduit are described. Verify physical plausibility: mantel height 48 in., mirror 72×48 in., mirror bottom +36 in., distance mantel to window 13 ft, mantel to east wall 3 ft, loose floorboard 2 ft east of hearth. Confirm provenance statements (brads, diary behind mirror, brass key under floorboard). Craft checks: maintain tension and not overexplain; keep Lena's investigative approach clear and plausible. Flag any contradictions or craft issues and indicate whether the scene passes or list required rewrites.

That is in addition to your standing instructions above, not instead of them.
If it states a story fact that is not in your packet — a name, a measurement, a
quotation, a piece of history — that fact has not been checked against the index by
anyone. Ask about it or establish it yourself in the state delta. Do not write it down
as though it were already true.

### scene-card  <novel/chapters/ch-01/chapter.yaml>

Scene s-001. Intent: Open in media res: Lena moves into Holloway House, establishes voice (rational, observational), discovers the Venetian mirror over the mantel and the diary tucked behind it, finds the brass key. Small, unnerving phenomena begin (sounds, a reflection that lags). The scene must set the house’s physical logic (angles, odd sightlines) and plant the principal objects and the narrator’s investigative approach.
Present: char-lena, loc-holloway-house, loc-parlor, obj-venetian-mirror, obj-diary, obj-brass-key
Target length: about 625 words.

### logline  <novel/outline/logline.md>

When Lena inherits an old house, an antique Venetian mirror and a hidden diary draw her into a precise, daylight-angled ritual that promises to free the woman who vanished there — but the mirror obeys geometry not mercy, and what is freed is not what she expects.

### entity-roster  <characters/, locations/, objects/>

Every entity that exists in this story. Only these ids may be used; if you need someone or something that is not here, say so rather than inventing an id.
- char-lena: Lena Ward, narrator, early thirties. A methodical, solitary woman (former library assistant) who inherits an old house and approaches the uncanny like a problem to be solved.
- char-archivist: Mr. Calder, the town archivist: patient, precise, mid-sixties. Knows the local records and is helpful but cautious about oral lore.
- char-mrs-haverford: Evelyn Haverford, next-door neighbor in her eighties. Knows house gossip and remembers the missing occupant. Gives warnings couched as small kindnesses.
- ghost-hannah: Hannah Hale (deceased), the presence bound to the Venetian mirror. Once vivacious, she vanished fifty years earlier; her diary survives. In life, she was meticulous about light and reflection; in death her behavior centers on mirrored surfaces and on repeating a missed final act.
- loc-holloway-house: Holloway House: a cramped, late-Victorian house on a hill outside a small town. It creaks with age and has odd sightlines inside — long mirrored parlor, tight attic, a tilted stairwell.
- loc-parlor: The front parlor on the ground floor of Holloway House. Large windows, faded wallpaper, and the antique Venetian mirror mounted above the mantel.
- loc-attic: A small, low-attic above the parlor reached by a narrow stair and locked with a brass key; it contains the house’s odd geometry — a shaft of light that can fall through a slat under certain angles.
- loc-town-archive: The county archive where Lena researches town records: a dim, smell-of-paper place with careful catalogs and one helpful archivist.
- obj-venetian-mirror: A large, old Venetian mirror above the parlor mantel. Its silvering has a faint, deliberate pattern — thin, almost hairline seams that are not damage but part of how it was made. It is the locus for the haunting.
- obj-diary: Hannah Hale’s small, habitually neat diary, written in a fine, cramped hand. Tucked behind the mirror. Contains dates, observations about angles of light, and a final ambiguous ritual outline.
- obj-brass-key: A small brass key found hidden under a loose floorboard in the parlor; it opens the attic door.
- obj-newspaper-clipping: A brittle newspaper clipping from 1972 about Hannah Hale’s disappearance; includes a photo showing the parlor and the mirror.
- obj-oil-lamp: An old oil lamp Lena buys for experiments in the parlor. Its flame is steadier and more yellow than modern lamps, used to reproduce the recorded light conditions.

### narrative-voice  <novel/style/voice.md>

Narration: first person, Lena, past tense. This was decided for the whole book before any of it was written and does not change.
Check your own sentences against it before you stage them. Mixing a collective "we" into a third-person narration, or slipping into present tense for a scene that feels immediate, is scored as a defect and is the most common one this system has produced: seven of nine consistency errors in a measured 18,000-word manuscript were exactly this.
If you think the story genuinely needs a different voice, propose the deviation — do not simply write it.

### world-rules  <world/rules.yaml>

These govern what is TRUE. They do not say what anyone KNOWS.
A character knows a rule only where canon says so; otherwise they may be ignorant of it, wrong about it, or in the middle of working it out — and if the story is about someone discovering one of these, writing it into their thoughts early is how that story gets destroyed.

- 1) The only supernatural mechanism in this story is reflection-conduction: certain mirrors, under specific geometric and lighting conditions, can act as conduits or repositories for a presence. No other ghost powers (telekinesis, omniscience) are allowed.
- 2) The Venetian mirror (obj-venetian-mirror) is special because of its silvering pattern; only it can hold Hannah's presence. Ordinary mirrors do not replicate the phenomena unless explicitly noted.
- 3) Light and angle matter. A precise alignment of light (time-of-day or a lamp placed at a marked position) must occur to 'activate' the conduit. The activation obeys ordinary geometric optics (lines of sight, reflection), and the narrator can calculate and reproduce it.
- 4) Physical objects obey normal physics. Breaking, moving or covering objects has immediate, ordinary consequences (shards, blocked sightlines). Breaking the mirror disperses the stored image/presence unpredictably but does not 'destroy' the metaphysical trace; the narrative must not show impossible physical outcomes.
- 5) Ritual language in the diary is ambiguous and fallible. It describes procedures that will produce an effect consistent with rules 1–4; it may omit moral cautions. Any consequences that follow must be deducible from the diary plus the mirror/light rules, not from arbitrary supernatural fiat.
- 6) Identity transfer is possible only through the mirror-conduit under the activation conditions. Such transfers are constrained: the conduit swaps or binds the reflected and reflecting subject according to the mirror’s geometry and cannot create or annihilate independent souls.

## The draft

I arrived with the van half-empty and the house already choosing its sounds. The parlor took my boxes with the same measured indifference: a long room with tall windows, faded wallpaper, and a mantel that sat four feet off the floor. The Venetian mirror above it was six feet wide by four feet tall; its lower edge began three feet above the mantel, so the glass started seven feet from the floor. The windows faced east; from the mantel to the nearest window opening it was thirteen feet, and the mantel’s right edge lay three feet from the east wall where the narrow stair rose.

I set down the last box, untied my tape, and drew the room on the back of an envelope — a rectangle for the mirror, a line for the windows, a dot where the hearth still smelled of old coal. In my sketch I wrote the numbers in a neat column: mantel 48 in., mirror 72×48 in., mirror bottom +36 in. I measured that by eye and with the cheap tape from my toolbox because these are the sorts of things that matter later.

The mirror was nailed to the mantel with old iron brads. I could hear the brads scrape faintly when I rocked the frame forward; the sound made me think of a hinge and a breath. I slid a putty knife under the bottom edge between the brads and eased the glass forward until the frame scraped the plaster. Behind it, folded flat against the wall, was a small diary: neat, narrow, the sort of book that had been written in with a very small, very steady hand.

I palmed the diary and felt the grain of its cover while the mirror returned to its place with a soft, rustling click. When I opened the book the handwriting ran on tight lines about angles and lamps and the way a slice of light would travel across the floor in March. I read one line aloud without meaning to: "Measure the angle at noon; do not trust the hour by the clock." The writing sat there like an instruction and a warning at once.

I wanted to check the floorboards because a house that keeps secrets often hides keys where a person might kneel to look for them. Two feet east of the hearth I found a plank that rode up under the heel when I stepped on it. A screwdriver pried the board loose and under it lay a small brass key, dull with age but warm from my hand the moment I picked it up.

There was a tapping then, very faint and regular, as if someone were turning a page behind the other side of the wall. It was not the settling that I’d expected; it had a rhythm — one-two, pause, one-two — and when I put my palm flat on the plaster I could feel the tiny modulation through the wood.

Back in front of the mantel I did a small experiment: I held my hand at a point I had marked on the sketch — seven inches left of center, at roughly the height of the mirror’s lower edge — and lifted it slowly. The reflection followed, but not perfectly. For a fraction of a second the glass showed my hand a beat after my hand had moved, as if the mirror were watching my gesture through a slow feed.

I closed the diary and let the brass key sit on top of it. The house hummed around me like an engine idling. I decided then to test the optics properly: precise measures, lamp angles, a repeatable note on where the lag happened. I made a note in the margin of the envelope and, as I packed the putty knife back into the toolbox, I felt the first, clean obligation of a problem I could solve.

I arrived with the van half-empty and the house already choosing its sounds. The parlor took my boxes with the same measured indifference: a long room with tall windows, faded wallpaper, and a mantel that sat four feet off the floor. The Venetian mirror above it was six feet wide by four feet tall; its lower edge began three feet above the mantel, so the glass started seven feet from the floor. The windows faced east; from the mantel to the nearest window opening it was thirteen feet, and the mantel’s right edge lay three feet from the east wall where the narrow stair rose.

I set down the last box, untied my tape, and drew the room on the back of an envelope — a rectangle for the mirror, a line for the windows, a dot where the hearth still smelled of old coal. In my sketch I wrote the numbers in a neat column: mantel 48 in., mirror 72×48 in., mirror bottom +36 in. I measured that by eye and with the cheap tape from my toolbox because these are the sorts of things that matter later.

The mirror was nailed to the mantel with old iron brads. I could hear the brads scrape faintly when I rocked the frame forward; the sound made me think of a hinge and a breath. I slid a putty knife under the bottom edge between the brads and eased the glass forward until the frame scraped the plaster. Behind it, folded flat against the wall, was a small diary: neat, narrow, the sort of book that had been written in with a very small, very steady hand.

I palmed the diary and felt the grain of its cover while the mirror returned to its place with a soft, rustling click. When I opened the book the handwriting ran on tight lines about angles and lamps and the way a slice of light would travel across the floor in March. I read one line aloud without meaning to: "Measure the angle at noon; do not trust the hour by the clock." The writing sat there like an instruction and a warning at once.

I wanted to check the floorboards because a house that keeps secrets often hides keys where a person might kneel to look for them. Two feet east of the hearth I found a plank that rode up under the heel when I stepped on it. A screwdriver pried the board loose and under it lay a small brass key, dull with age but warm from my hand the moment I picked it up.

There was a tapping then, very faint and regular, as if someone were turning a page behind the other side of the wall. It was not the settling that I’d expected; it had a rhythm — one-two, pause, one-two — and when I put my palm flat on the plaster I could feel the tiny modulation through the wood.

Back in front of the mantel I did a small experiment: I held my hand at a point I had marked on the sketch — seven inches left of center, at roughly the height of the mirror’s lower edge — and lifted it slowly. The reflection followed, but not perfectly. For a fraction of a second the glass showed my hand a beat after my hand had moved, as if the mirror were watching my gesture through a slow feed.

I closed the diary and let the brass key sit on top of it. The house hummed around me like an engine idling. I decided then to test the optics properly: precise measures, lamp angles, a repeatable note on where the lag happened. I made a note in the margin of the envelope and, as I packed the putty knife back into the toolbox, I felt the first, clean obligation of a problem I could solve.

I went to the archive because paper keeps its promises longer than people do. Mr. Calder worked with gloves and a lamp and the patience of someone who has watched handwriting fade into rumor. He pushed a small folder across his desk and said, as if reading from the edge of a map, "Holloway Gazette, mid‑March 1972 — photograph of Holloway House. Box 4, Folder 12. Accession HA‑1972‑03." He let me lift the brittle clipping. The caption beneath the grainy photograph named the day: March 14, 1972.

The picture showed the mantel and the mirror in the same shape I'd learned by touch: the hairline seam across the silvering, the tall east windows throwing a wedge of light onto the floor. Mr. Calder tapped the margin with a clean finger. "We don't have much more than this and the report," he said. "If you want recollection, ask the neighbours."

Mrs. Haverford brewed the kettle as if she were pouring memory into cups. She watched me over her spectacles, and when I told her about the clipping she pursed her lips and offered what a town keeps in pockets: small certainties and larger warnings. "Hannah fussed with her glass," she said. "She used to warn people about the seam — said you could feed a thing into it if you weren't careful. Mind the seam, love — and don't light it at noon." She bisected the words like a housewife folding sheet linen and set them before me.

Back at the parlor I spread the diary on the mantel and read until the ink began to look like instructions rather than memory. Two entries repeated the same odd, technical image and gave it dates in March. One, headed March 9, 1972, said, "At the seam the glass receives what the room offers; mark the joint and do not let the light strike the wrong edge." Another, dated March 21, 1972, read, "Note the angle at the sill; when the light cuts the sill aright the seam answers and will not be denied." The book had also once advised, in the language of someone who trusted geometry over timepieces, that the midday light mattered more than the clock on the wall.

Those three notes—archive, neighbour, diary—snapped into a working shape. The photograph fixed a date and showed the seam; Mrs. Haverford supplied the folk phrasing; the diary insisted that the seam and an "angle at the sill" were recurring, intentional observations. If the silvering included a seam that functioned like a channel, then a beam arriving at a particular declination could be the activating condition. That activation would obey optics, not omen: an aligned ray traveling to the seam, unbroken, might produce the reflection effects I had already noticed.

I made the hypothesis explicit and wrote down two simple, falsifiable predictions. Prediction one: reproduce the March sun's angle with my oil lamp and the mirror will show the lagged echo again and an intensified shimmer at the seam. I set a tentative placement on the sketch — lamp six feet from the mantel, flame roughly eighteen inches above the hearth, and aligned seven inches left of the mirror's center mark. Prediction two: interrupting the reflective path by covering the seam with an opaque strip or placing a board across the sill will stop the lag and the shimmer, proving the effect needs an unobstructed reflective route.

I measured the six feet with the cheap tape and made the mark seven inches left of centre in pencil on the envelope I kept with the diary. The protractor from my toolbox was ready; the oil lamp was already ordered online. Mrs. Haverford's string of warning — "Mind the seam, love — and don't light it at noon" — sounded less like superstition than like a neighbourly inversion of caution: a note to be observed and also tested. The next clear morning I planned to set the lamp at my pencilled spots, measure the angle across the sill, and watch what the glass did when the light cut it true.

I arrived with the van half-empty and the house already choosing its sounds. The parlor took my boxes with the same measured indifference: a long room with tall windows, faded wallpaper, and a mantel that sat four feet off the floor. The Venetian mirror above it was six feet wide by four feet tall; its lower edge began three feet above the mantel, so the glass started seven feet from the floor. The windows faced east; from the mantel to the nearest window opening it was thirteen feet, and the mantel’s right edge lay three feet from the east wall where the narrow stair rose.

I set down the last box, untied my tape, and drew the room on the back of an envelope — a rectangle for the mirror, a line for the windows, a dot where the hearth still smelled of old coal. In my sketch I wrote the numbers in a neat column: mantel 48 in., mirror 72×48 in., mirror bottom +36 in. I measured that by eye and with the cheap tape from my toolbox because these are the sorts of things that matter later.

The mirror was nailed to the mantel with old iron brads. I could hear the brads scrape faintly when I rocked the frame forward; the sound made me think of a hinge and a breath. I slid a putty knife under the bottom edge between the brads and eased the glass forward until the frame scraped the plaster. Behind it, folded flat against the wall, was a small diary: neat, narrow, the sort of book that had been written in with a very small, very steady hand.

I palmed the diary and felt the grain of its cover while the mirror returned to its place with a soft, rustling click. When I opened the book the handwriting ran on tight lines about angles and lamps and the way a slice of light would travel across the floor in March. I read one line aloud without meaning to: "Measure the angle at noon; do not trust the hour by the clock." The writing sat there like an instruction and a warning at once.

I wanted to check the floorboards because a house that keeps secrets often hides keys where a person might kneel to look for them. Two feet east of the hearth I found a plank that rode up under the heel when I stepped on it. A screwdriver pried the board loose and under it lay a small brass key, dull with age but warm from my hand the moment I picked it up.

There was a tapping then, very faint and regular, as if someone were turning a page behind the other side of the wall. It was not the settling that I’d expected; it had a rhythm — one-two, pause, one-two — and when I put my palm flat on the plaster I could feel the tiny modulation through the wood.

Back in front of the mantel I did a small experiment: I held my hand at a point I had marked on the sketch — seven inches left of center, at roughly the height of the mirror’s lower edge — and lifted it slowly. The reflection followed, but not perfectly. For a fraction of a second the glass showed my hand a beat after my hand had moved, as if the mirror were watching my gesture through a slow feed.

I closed the diary and let the brass key sit on top of it. The house hummed around me like an engine idling. I decided then to test the optics properly: precise measures, lamp angles, a repeatable note on where the lag happened. I went to the archive because paper keeps its promises longer than people do. Mr. Calder worked with gloves and a lamp and the patience of someone who has watched handwriting fade into rumor. He pushed a small folder across his desk and said, as if reading from the edge of a map, "Holloway Gazette, mid‑March 1972 — photograph of Holloway House. Box 4, Folder 12. Accession HA‑1972‑03." He let me lift the brittle clipping. The caption beneath the grainy photograph named the day: March 14, 1972.

The picture showed the mantel and the mirror in the same shape I'd learned by touch: the hairline seam across the silvering, the tall east windows throwing a wedge of light onto the floor. Mr. Calder tapped the margin with a clean finger. "We don't have much more than this and the report," he said. "If you want recollection, ask the neighbours."

Mrs. Haverford brewed the kettle as if she were pouring memory into cups. She watched me over her spectacles, and when I told her about the clipping she pursed her lips and offered what a town keeps in pockets: small certainties and larger warnings. "Hannah fussed with her glass," she said. "She used to warn people about the seam — said you could feed a thing into it if you weren't careful. Mind the seam, love — and don't light it at noon." She bisected the words like a housewife folding sheet linen and set them before me.

Back at the parlor I spread the diary on the mantel and read until the ink began to look like instructions rather than memory. Two entries repeated the same odd, technical image and gave it dates in March. One, headed March 9, 1972, said, "At the seam the glass receives what the room offers; mark the joint and do not let the light strike the wrong edge." Another, dated March 21, 1972, read, "Note the angle at the sill; when the light cuts the sill aright the seam answers and will not be denied." The book had also once advised, in the language of someone who trusted geometry over timepieces, that the midday light mattered more than the clock on the wall.

Those three notes—archive, neighbour, diary—snapped into a working shape. The photograph fixed a date and showed the seam; Mrs. Haverford supplied the folk phrasing; the diary insisted that the seam and an "angle at the sill" were recurring, intentional observations. If the silvering included a seam that functioned like a channel, then a beam arriving at a particular declination could be the activating condition. That activation would obey optics, not omen: an aligned ray traveling to the seam, unbroken, might produce the reflection effects I had already noticed.

I made the hypothesis explicit and wrote down two simple, falsifiable predictions. Prediction one: reproduce the March sun's angle with my oil lamp and the mirror will show the lagged echo again and an intensified shimmer at the seam. I set a tentative placement on the sketch — lamp six feet from the mantel, flame roughly eighteen inches above the hearth, and aligned seven inches left of the mirror's center mark. Prediction two: interrupting the reflective path by covering the seam with an opaque strip or placing a board across the sill will stop the lag and the shimmer, proving the effect needs an unobstructed reflective route.

I measured the six feet with the cheap tape and made the mark seven inches left of centre in pencil on the envelope I kept with the diary. The protractor from my toolbox was ready; the oil lamp was already ordered online. Mrs. Haverford's string of warning — "Mind the seam, love — and don't light it at noon" — sounded less like superstition than like a neighbourly inversion of caution: a note to be observed and also tested. The next clear morning I planned to set the lamp at my pencilled spots, measure the angle across the sill, and watch what the glass did when the light cut it true.

In my sketch I wrote the numbers in a neat column: mantel 48 in., mirror 72×48 in., mirror bottom +36 in. I measured that by eye and with the cheap tape from my toolbox because these are the sorts of things that matter later.

The mirror was nailed to the mantel with old iron brads. I could hear the brads scrape faintly when I rocked the frame forward; the sound made me think of a hinge and a breath. I slid a putty knife under the bottom edge between the brads and eased the glass forward until the frame scraped the plaster. Behind it, folded flat against the wall, was a small diary: neat, narrow, the sort of book that had been written in with a very small, very steady hand.

I palmed the diary and felt the grain of its cover while the mirror returned to its place with a soft, rustling click. When I opened the book the handwriting ran on tight lines about angles and lamps and the way a slice of light would travel across the floor in March. I read one line aloud without meaning to: "Measure the angle at noon; do not trust the hour by the clock." The writing sat there like an instruction and a warning at once.

I wanted to check the floorboards because a house that keeps secrets often hides keys where a person might kneel to look for them. Two feet east of the hearth I found a plank that rode up under the heel when I stepped on it. A screwdriver pried the board loose and under it lay a small brass key, dull with age but warm from my hand the moment I picked it up.

There was a tapping then, very faint and regular, as if someone were turning a page behind the other side of the wall. It was not the settling that I’d expected; it had a rhythm — one-two, pause, one-two — and when I put my palm flat on the plaster I could feel the tiny modulation through the wood.

Back in front of the mantel I did a small experiment: I held my hand at a point I had marked on the sketch — seven inches left of center, at roughly the height of the mirror’s lower edge — and lifted it slowly. The reflection followed, but not perfectly. For a fraction of a second the glass showed my hand a beat after my hand had moved, as if the mirror were watching my gesture through a slow feed.

I closed the diary and let the brass key sit on top of it. The house hummed around me like an engine idling. I decided then to test the optics properly: precise measures, lamp angles, a repeatable note on where the lag happened. I made a note in the margin of the envelope and, as I packed the putty knife back into the toolbox, I felt the first, clean obligation of a problem I could solve.

## The draft

I set the oil lamp six feet from the mantel and propped the wick so the flame rode roughly eighteen inches above the hearth. I measured the six feet again because measuring was the part of this that felt like control, then I pencilled a small cross on the floor seven inches to the left of the mirror’s centre and taped a strip of envelope paper there to hold the mark.

When everything was where the sketch said it should be I struck a match. The lamp threw a softer, more yellow cone than an electric bulb; it felt as if I had lit an old photograph. The seam in the silvering caught it first and, for a heartbeat that was both longer and too short, the glass answered with an intensified shimmer along that hairline joint. My hand in front of the glass registered a fraction of a second sooner than its reflection — the lag I'd written down as a prediction — and where the seam ran the reflected surface wavered like a skin being plucked.

The reflection was not the room I was sitting in. In the glass the narrow stair descended on the left while, behind me, the real stair rose on the right. Light in the mirror had a colder edge, a blue that did not belong to my lamp; the reflected banister cast a shadow where the real banister made none. The impossible geometry sat there like an answer to something I had only started to ask.

I followed the diary's careful language because the diary had been precise where people were not. Tucked into the margin, dated March 24, 1972, were three short directives I read aloud, as if hearing them aloud would make them obey me as well as the paper:

"Mark the seam."

"Place the flame where the sill is cut."

"Speak her name and give the leaving."

I took the brass key from the mantel—still dull where my thumb had warmed it earlier—and turned it in the attic hatch's rim lock. The catch resisted with an old sigh and then gave. The stair to the attic was narrow and pitched; I climbed into a low, cedar-dark space where dust made the air taste like dry paper. The attic ceiling brushed my forearms; the roof slants made the room feel smaller than the house below.

A single slat on the north rafter was split from edge to edge and left a vertical gap of about two inches. It sat two feet from the hatch and ten feet from the east-facing window, and when I knelt on the hatch lip a thin shaft of lamp-light threaded through the gap and struck the attic floor in a line that aimed back toward the mantel. The diary's phrase about the angle at the sill stopped being an abstraction when I saw that line: the house already gave the ray the path the paper described.

Back in the parlor I pressed a fingertip to the glass where the seam ran. The skin of dust shifted under my touch and, beneath that, something moved to match it. Hannah came then — not a storm but a sequence: she tapped once, twice, three times along the inside of the frame; she did it in precise, patient counts, as if enumerating steps. Her mouth formed one slow word. I read it because there is no other polite thing to do with an apparition that mouths a syllable: "light."

She lifted a finger and dragged it along the glass. The dust rearranged at her touch and, in the darkened trail, the letters of a single word appeared as if written by the absence she left: free.

I held the match between two fingers. The diary lay open to the three directives and the lamp burned where I had placed it. My hand hovered over the wick and, for the first time since I started cataloguing the house, I felt the shape of a decision: follow the outline exactly now, or refuse the ritual and see what the conduit does if left unanswered. Either choice would change what the house meant. I did not move.

I went to the archive because paper keeps its promises longer than people do. Mr. Calder worked with gloves and a lamp and the patience of someone who has watched handwriting fade into rumor. He pushed a small folder across his desk and said, as if reading from the edge of a map, "Holloway Gazette, mid‑March 1972 — photograph of Holloway House. Box 4, Folder 12. Accession HA‑1972‑03." He let me lift the brittle clipping. The caption beneath the grainy photograph named the day: March 14, 1972.

The picture showed the mantel and the mirror in the same shape I'd learned by touch: the hairline seam across the silvering, the tall east windows throwing a wedge of light onto the floor. Mr. Calder tapped the margin with a clean finger. "We don't have much more than this and the report," he said. "If you want recollection, ask the neighbours."

Mrs. Haverford brewed the kettle as if she were pouring memory into cups. She watched me over her spectacles, and when I told her about the clipping she pursed her lips and offered what a town keeps in pockets: small certainties and larger warnings. "Hannah fussed with her glass," she said. "She used to warn people about the seam — said you could feed a thing into it if you weren't careful. Mind the seam, love — and don't light it at noon." She bisected the words like a housewife folding sheet linen and set them before me.

Back at the parlor I spread the diary on the mantel and read until the ink began to look like instructions rather than memory. Two entries repeated the same odd, technical image and gave it dates in March. One, headed March 9, 1972, said, "At the seam the glass receives what the room offers; mark the joint and do not let the light strike the wrong edge." Another, dated March 21, 1972, read, "Note the angle at the sill; when the light cuts the sill aright the seam answers and will not be denied." The book had also once advised, in the language of someone who trusted geometry over timepieces, that the midday light mattered more than the clock on the wall.

Those three notes—archive, neighbour, diary—snapped into a working shape. The photograph fixed a date and showed the seam; Mrs. Haverford supplied the folk phrasing; the diary insisted that the seam and an "angle at the sill" were recurring, intentional observations. If the silvering included a seam that functioned like a channel, then a beam arriving at a particular declination could be the activating condition. That activation would obey optics, not omen: an aligned ray traveling to the seam, unbroken, might produce the reflection effects I had already noticed.

I made the hypothesis explicit and wrote down two simple, falsifiable predictions. Prediction one: reproduce the March sun's angle with my oil lamp and the mirror will show the lagged echo again and an intensified shimmer at the seam. I set a tentative placement on the sketch — lamp six feet from the mantel, flame roughly eighteen inches above the hearth, and aligned seven inches left of the mirror's center mark. Prediction two: interrupting the reflective path by covering the seam with an opaque strip or placing a board across the sill will stop the lag and the shimmer, proving the effect needs an unobstructed reflective route.

I measured the six feet with the cheap tape and made the mark seven inches left of centre in pencil on the envelope I kept with the diary. The protractor from my toolbox was ready; the oil lamp was already ordered online. Mrs. Haverford's string of warning — "Mind the seam, love — and don't light it at noon" — sounded less like superstition than like a neighbourly inversion of caution: a note to be observed and also tested. The next clear morning I planned to set the lamp at my pencilled spots, measure the angle across the sill, and watch what the glass did when the light cut it true.

In my sketch I wrote the numbers in a neat column: mantel 48 in., mirror 72×48 in., mirror bottom +36 in. I measured that by eye and with the cheap tape from my toolbox because these are the sorts of things that matter later.

The mirror was nailed to the mantel with old iron brads. I could hear the brads scrape faintly when I rocked the frame forward; the sound made me think of a hinge and a breath. I slid a putty knife under the bottom edge between the brads and eased the glass forward until the frame scraped the plaster. Behind it, folded flat against the wall, was a small diary: neat, narrow, the sort of book that had been written in with a very small, very steady hand.

I palmed the diary and felt the grain of its cover while the mirror returned to its place with a soft, rustling click. When I opened the book the handwriting ran on tight lines about angles and lamps and the way a slice of light would travel across the floor in March. I read one line aloud without meaning to: "Measure the angle at noon; do not trust the hour by the clock." The writing sat there like an instruction and a warning at once.

I wanted to check the floorboards because a house that keeps secrets often hides keys where a person might kneel to look for them. Two feet east of the hearth I found a plank that rode up under the heel when I stepped on it. A screwdriver pried the board loose and under it lay a small brass key, dull with age but warm from my hand the moment I picked it up.

There was a tapping then, very faint and regular, as if someone were turning a page behind the other side of the wall. It was not the settling that I’d expected; it had a rhythm — one-two, pause, one-two — and when I put my palm flat on the plaster I could feel the tiny modulation through the wood.

Back in front of the mantel I did a small experiment: I held my hand at a point I had marked on the sketch — seven inches left of center, at roughly the height of the mirror’s lower edge — and lifted it slowly. The reflection followed, but not perfectly. For a fraction of a second the glass showed my hand a beat after my hand had moved, as if the mirror were watching my gesture through a slow feed.

I closed the diary and let the brass key sit on top of it. The house hummed around me like an engine idling. I decided then to test the optics properly: precise measures, lamp angles, a repeatable note on where the lag happened. I made a note in the margin of the envelope and, as I packed the putty knife back into the toolbox, I felt the first, clean obligation of a problem I could solve.

I set the oil lamp six feet from the mantel and propped the wick so the flame rode roughly eighteen inches above the hearth. I measured the six feet again because measuring was the part of this that felt like control, then I pencilled a small cross on the floor seven inches to the left of the mirror’s centre and taped a strip of envelope paper there to hold the mark.

When everything was where the sketch said it should be I struck a match. The lamp threw a softer, more yellow cone than an electric bulb; it felt as if I had lit an old photograph. The seam in the silvering caught it first and, for a heartbeat that was both longer and too short, the glass answered with an intensified shimmer along that hairline joint. My hand in front of the glass registered a fraction of a second sooner than its reflection — the lag I'd written down as a prediction — and where the seam ran the reflected surface wavered like a skin being plucked.

The reflection was not the room I was sitting in. In the glass the narrow stair descended on the left while, behind me, the real stair rose on the right. Light in the mirror had a colder edge, a blue that did not belong to my lamp; the reflected banister cast a shadow where the real banister made none. The impossible geometry sat there like an answer to something I had only started to ask.

I followed the diary's careful language because the diary had been precise where people were not. Tucked into the margin, dated March 24, 1972, were three short directives I read aloud, as if hearing them aloud would make them obey me as well as the paper:

"Mark the seam."

"Place the flame where the sill is cut."

"Speak her name and give the leaving."

I took the brass key from the mantel—still dull where my thumb had warmed it earlier—and turned it in the attic hatch's rim lock. The catch resisted with an old sigh and then gave. The stair to the attic was narrow and pitched; I climbed into a low, cedar-dark space where dust made the air taste like dry paper. The attic ceiling brushed my forearms; the roof slants made the room feel smaller than the house below.

A single slat on the north rafter was split from edge to edge and left a vertical gap of about two inches. It sat two feet from the hatch and ten feet from the east-facing window, and when I knelt on the hatch lip a thin shaft of lamp-light threaded through the gap and struck the attic floor in a line that aimed back toward the mantel. The diary's phrase about the angle at the sill stopped being an abstraction when I saw that line: the house already gave the ray the path the paper described.

Back in the parlor I pressed a fingertip to the glass where the seam ran. The skin of dust under my fingertip was unmoved but, in the mirror's other side, something matched my touch. She lifted a finger and dragged it along the glass. In the mirror's other side the dust seemed to part where her finger slid; in that reflected seam the darkened trail spelled a single word: "free." The dust on my side of the frame did not move.

Hannah came then — not a storm but a sequence: she tapped once, twice, three times along the inside of the frame; she did it in precise, patient counts, as if enumerating steps. Her mouth formed one slow word. I read it because there is no other polite thing to do with an apparition that mouths a syllable: "light."

My fingers closed around the match. I struck it, lifted the flame to the wick, and said, plainly, "Hannah Hale." Then I read the diary line and spoke it aloud to the room, slow and deliberate: "Speak her name and give the leaving." The wick took; the lamp settled into its cone of light where I had measured it. The mirror watched, and whatever answered to names and measures waited without hurrying.

I arrived with the van half-empty and the house already choosing its sounds. The parlor took my boxes with the same measured indifference: a long room with tall windows, faded wallpaper, and a mantel that sat four feet off the floor. The Venetian mirror above it was six feet wide by four feet tall; its lower edge began three feet above the mantel, so the glass started seven feet from the floor. The windows faced east; from the mantel to the nearest window opening it was thirteen feet, and the mantel’s right edge lay three feet from the east wall where the narrow stair rose.

I set down the last box, untied my tape, and drew the room on the back of an envelope — a rectangle for the mirror, a line for the windows, a dot where the hearth still smelled of old coal. In my sketch I wrote the numbers in a neat column: mantel 48 in., mirror 72×48 in., mirror bottom +36 in. I measured that by eye and with the cheap tape from my toolbox because these are the sorts of things that matter later.

The mirror was nailed to the mantel with old iron brads. I could hear the brads scrape faintly when I rocked the frame forward; the sound made me think of a hinge and a breath. I slid a putty knife under the bottom edge between the brads and eased the glass forward until the frame scraped the plaster. Behind it, folded flat against the wall, was a small diary: neat, narrow, the sort of book that had been written in with a very small, very steady hand.

I went to the archive because paper keeps its promises longer than people do. Mr. Calder worked with gloves and a lamp and the patience of someone who has watched handwriting fade into rumor. He pushed a small folder across his desk and said, as if reading from the edge of a map, "Holloway Gazette, mid‑March 1972 — photograph of Holloway House. Box 4, Folder 12. Accession HA‑1972‑03." He let me lift the brittle clipping. The caption beneath the grainy photograph named the day: March 14, 1972.

The picture showed the mantel and the mirror in the same shape I'd learned by touch: the hairline seam across the silvering, the tall east windows throwing a wedge of light onto the floor. Mr. Calder tapped the margin with a clean finger. "We don't have much more than this and the report," he said. "If you want recollection, ask the neighbours."

Mrs. Haverford brewed the kettle as if she were pouring memory into cups. She watched me over her spectacles, and when I told her about the clipping she pursed her lips and offered what a town keeps in pockets: small certainties and larger warnings. "Hannah fussed with her glass," she said. "She used to warn people about the seam — said you could feed a thing into it if you weren't careful. Mind the seam, love — and don't light it at noon." She bisected the words like a housewife folding sheet linen and set them before me.

Back at the parlor I spread the diary on the mantel and read until the ink began to look like instructions rather than memory. Two entries repeated the same odd, technical image and gave it dates in March. One, headed March 9, 1972, said, "At the seam the glass receives what the room offers; mark the joint and do not let the light strike the wrong edge." Another, dated March 21, 1972, read, "Note the angle at the sill; when the light cuts the sill aright the seam answers and will not be denied." The book had also once advised, in the language of someone who trusted geometry over timepieces, that the midday light mattered more than the clock on the wall.

## Second axis: the writing itself

The nineteen subtypes above are consistency errors, and they are one of the two numbers
this system is scored on. The other is quality, judged on rubrics that penalise things no
consistency subtype can express — and that is where our deficit actually is: measured on
the same task, our length score was the best in the field and our quality score was 0.5 to
0.8 points below the frontier on a five-point scale, where one point of quality is worth
ten points of the mean.

Two of the worst defects found by reading our finished manuscripts were invisible to a
consistency gate by construction. The story **had no ending** — the final scene was a
confrontation that named nobody and closed on "Not yet. There is enough for a warrant" —
and an unresolved ending contradicts nothing, so there was no subtype to report it as. And
the scenes **restate each other**: same content, different words, so no textual comparison
sees it, and it is not a contradiction. It is what makes a long story feel padded.

So report those with `write_craft_finding`. The checks, each naming the scored dimension
that penalises it:

- **off_brief** (can block) — the scene does something other than what its card said it would, or drifts off what the task actually asked for — a required element of the premise handled as background, or a scene that services a thread the task never mentioned.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Relevance — "content highly relevant and fully applicable to the user's request"; LongStoryEval Expectation Fulfillment — "how effectively the story meets the readers' expectations based on the premise and genres"
- **restates_prior_scene** (can block) — the scene delivers information, a realisation or a beat the reader already has. Not the same words — the same content: a suspicion re-voiced, a relationship re-explained, a clue re-found. This is what makes a long story feel padded rather than long, and verbatim overlap does not detect it.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Breadth and Depth — "seriously lacking breadth and depth with minimal information"; LongBench-Write Reading Experience — "boring and hard to understand"
- **nothing_changes** (can block) — the situation at the end of the scene is the situation at the start. Nobody knows something new, owes something new, has lost something or has decided. Name the state at the open and the state at the close; if you cannot name a difference, that is the finding.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Coherence — "disorganized structure with no coherence"; LongBench-Write Breadth and Depth
- **internal_incoherence** (can block) — the scene contradicts itself, with both halves inside this draft — a detail stated one way early and another way late, a character reacting to something they have not been told in this scene, a sequence that cannot have happened in the order given. This needs no index at all, which is why it is inexcusable to miss.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Accuracy — "content with numerous errors and highly misleading"; LongBench-Write Coherence
- **ending_not_delivered** (can block) — the last scene stops instead of ending. The question the premise poses is not answered on the page: who, how, and — in a mystery — how the impossibility was possible. An arrangement of clues from which a reader could deduce the answer is not the answer. Name the question the premise poses and quote where the draft answers it; if you cannot quote that, the ending is not delivered.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Accuracy and Relevance; LongStoryEval Expectation Fulfillment
- **summary_not_scene** (warning only) — events reported rather than dramatised — a paragraph that says an argument happened instead of letting it happen. Compression is legitimate and necessary; a scene whose central beat is summarised is not compressed, it is skipped.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Reading Experience; LongStoryEval Writing and Language — "the writing style's ability to engage and captivate readers"
- **thin_for_its_length** (warning only) — the scene is near its word target and carries one beat's worth of content, padded with restatement, weather, or interiority that repeats itself. The grader penalises this and the length score does not reward it.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Breadth and Depth
- **costless_conflict** (warning only) — a conflict resolved without costing anybody anything specific. Partial and temporary resolutions are fine; free ones read as unearned.
    penalised by: LongStoryEval Emotional Impact — "the story's ability to evoke strong and deep emotional impact"
- **theme_stated** (warning only) — a sentence that explains what the story means, rather than a choice that tests it. Quote the sentence — it is almost always removable without loss.
    penalised by: LongStoryEval Themes — "how well the themes are explored throughout the story"
- **flat_diction** (warning only) — constructions repeating within the scene, filter verbs standing in for perception ("she felt that", "he realised that"), abstraction where a concrete detail belongs, or sentence rhythm that does not move with the tension.
    penalised by: LongStoryEval Writing and Language; LongBench-Write Clarity — "confusing expression with minimal details"

    penalised by: LongStoryEval Expectation Fulfillment; LongBench-Write Relevance

Two rules, both enforced by the tool rather than left to your judgement:

Only these may be **error** and therefore cost the writer a round: off_brief, restates_prior_scene, nothing_changes, internal_incoherence, ending_not_delivered.
Everything else is a warning — it reaches the writer and costs nothing. That asymmetry is
deliberate: a craft judgement a reader could reasonably disagree with must not be able to
hold up a scene.

And a blocking craft finding needs **checkable evidence**, in the shape the check names.
Either two verbatim quotes (this draft, and the earlier passage it repeats or the half of
itself it contradicts), or a named state pair — what is true when the scene opens and what
is true when it closes. `nothing_changes` is precisely the claim that you cannot name a
difference, so name both halves and let the pair be the evidence. If you cannot produce
the evidence, you have an impression: report it as a warning, which is a perfectly useful
thing to do.

`suggestion` is mandatory on every craft finding, warnings included. The writer cannot see
the manuscript, the index or the rubric. A craft note without an instruction is a complaint
it can only answer by guessing, and a guessed craft repair damages prose that was working —
which is not hypothetical: a run whose findings the writer could not act on scored 8.4
points below one with fewer, better ones.

At most two craft findings can block one round, whatever you report. Consistency comes
first when both are present: it is counted by name and craft is not. So if you have three
craft blockers, the third is a warning — pick the two that most damage the scene.

### previous-scene  <novel/chapters/ch-01/scenes/s-003.md>

I set the oil lamp six feet from the mantel and propped the wick so the flame rode roughly eighteen inches above the hearth. I measured the six feet again because measuring was the part of this that felt like control, then I pencilled a small cross on the floor seven inches to the left of the mirror’s centre and taped a strip of envelope paper there to hold the mark.

When everything was where the sketch said it should be I struck a match. The lamp threw a softer, more yellow cone than an electric bulb; it felt as if I had lit an old photograph. The seam in the silvering caught it first and, for a heartbeat that was both longer and too short, the glass answered with an intensified shimmer along that hairline joint. My hand in front of the glass registered a fraction of a second sooner than its reflection — the lag I'd written down as a prediction — and where the seam ran the reflected surface wavered like a skin being plucked.

The reflection was not the room I was sitting in. In the glass the narrow stair descended on the left while, behind me, the real stair rose on the right. Light in the mirror had a colder edge, a blue that did not belong to my lamp; the reflected banister cast a shadow where the real banister made none. The impossible geometry sat there like an answer to something I had only started to ask.

I followed the diary's careful language because the diary had been precise where people were not. Tucked into the margin, dated March 24, 1972, were three short directives I read aloud, as if hearing them aloud would make them obey me as well as the paper:

"Mark the seam."

"Place the flame where the sill is cut."

"Speak her name and give the leaving."

I took the brass key from the mantel—still dull where my thumb had warmed it earlier—and turned it in the attic hatch's rim lock. The catch resisted with an old sigh and then gave. The stair to the attic was narrow and pitched; I climbed into a low, cedar-dark space where dust made the air taste like dry paper. The attic ceiling brushed my forearms; the roof slants made the room feel smaller than the house below.

A single slat on the north rafter was split from edge to edge and left a vertical gap of about two inches. It sat two feet from the hatch and ten feet from the east-facing window, and when I knelt on the hatch lip a thin shaft of lamp-light threaded through the gap and struck the attic floor in a line that aimed back toward the mantel. The diary's phrase about the angle at the sill stopped being an abstraction when I saw that line: the house already gave the ray the path the paper described.

Back in the parlor I pressed a fingertip to the glass where the seam ran. The skin of dust under my fingertip was unmoved but, in the mirror's other side, something matched my touch. She lifted a finger and dragged it along the glass. In the mirror's other side the dust seemed to part where her finger slid; in that reflected seam the darkened trail spelled a single word: "free." The dust on my side of the frame did not move.

Hannah came then — not a storm but a sequence: she tapped once, twice, three times along the inside of the frame; she did it in precise, patient counts, as if enumerating steps. Her mouth formed one slow word. I read it because there is no other polite thing to do with an apparition that mouths a syllable: "light."

My fingers closed around the match. I struck it, lifted the flame to the wick, and said, plainly, "Hannah Hale." Then I read the diary line and spoke it aloud to the room, slow and deliberate: "Speak her name and give the leaving." The wick took; the lamp settled into its cone of light where I had measured it. The mirror watched, and whatever answered to names and measures waited without hurrying.

I went to the archive because paper keeps its promises longer than people do. Mr. Calder worked with gloves and a lamp and the patience of someone who has watched handwriting fade into rumor. He pushed a small folder across his desk and said, as if reading from the edge of a map, "Holloway Gazette, mid‑March 1972 — photograph of Holloway House. Box 4, Folder 12. Accession HA‑1972‑03." He let me lift the brittle clipping. The caption beneath the grainy photograph named the day: March 14, 1972.

The picture showed the mantel and the mirror in the same shape I'd learned by touch: the hairline seam across the silvering, the tall east windows throwing a wedge of light onto the floor. Mr. Calder tapped the margin with a clean finger. "We don't have much more than this and the report," he said. "If you want recollection, ask the neighbours."

Mrs. Haverford brewed the kettle as if she were pouring memory into cups. She watched me over her spectacles, and when I told her about the clipping she pursed her lips and offered what a town keeps in pockets: small certainties and larger warnings. "Hannah fussed with her glass," she said. "She used to warn people about the seam — said you could feed a thing into it if you weren't careful. Mind the seam, love — and don't light it at noon." She bisected the words like a housewife folding sheet linen and set them before me.

Back at the parlor I spread the diary on the mantel and read until the ink began to look like instructions rather than memory. Two entries repeated the same odd, technical image and gave it dates in March. One, headed March 9, 1972, said, "At the seam the glass receives what the room offers; mark the joint and do not let the light strike the wrong edge." Another, dated March 21, 1972, read, "Note the angle at the sill; when the light cuts the sill aright the seam answers and will not be denied." The book had also once advised, in the language of someone who trusted geometry over timepieces, that the midday light mattered more than the clock on the wall.

Those three notes—archive, neighbour, diary—snapped into a working shape. The photograph fixed a date and showed the seam; Mrs. Haverford supplied the folk phrasing; the diary insisted that the seam and an "angle at the sill" were recurring, intentional observations. If the silvering included a seam that functioned like a channel, then a beam arriving at a particular declination could be the activating condition. That activation would obey optics, not omen: an aligned ray traveling to the seam, unbroken, might produce the reflection effects I had already noticed.

I made the hypothesis explicit and wrote down two simple, falsifiable predictions. Prediction one: reproduce the March sun's angle with my oil lamp and the mirror will show the lagged echo again and an intensified shimmer at the seam. I set a tentative placement on the sketch — lamp six feet from the mantel, flame roughly eighteen inches above the hearth, and aligned seven inches left of the mirror's center mark. Prediction two: interrupting the reflective path by covering the seam with an opaque strip or placing a board across the sill will stop the lag and the shimmer, proving the effect needs an unobstructed reflective route.

I measured the six feet with the cheap tape and made the mark seven inches left of centre in pencil on the envelope I kept with the diary. The protractor from my toolbox was ready; the oil lamp was already ordered online. Mrs. Haverford's string of warning — "Mind the seam, love — and don't light it at noon" — sounded less like superstition than like a neighbourly inversion of caution: a note to be observed and also tested. The next clear morning I planned to set the lamp at my pencilled spots, measure the angle across the sill, and watch what the glass did when the light cut it true.

I arrived with the van half-empty and the house already choosing its sounds. The parlor took my boxes with the same measured indifference: a long room with tall windows, faded wallpaper, and a mantel that sat four feet off the floor. The Venetian mirror above it was six feet wide by four feet tall; its lower edge began three feet above the mantel, so the glass started seven feet from the floor. The windows faced east; from the mantel to the nearest window opening it was thirteen feet, and the mantel’s right edge lay three feet from the east wall where the narrow stair rose.

I set down the last box, untied my tape, and drew the room on the back of an envelope — a rectangle for the mirror, a line for the windows, a dot where the hearth still smelled of old coal. In my sketch I wrote the numbers in a neat column: mantel 48 in., mirror 72×48 in., mirror bottom +36 in. I measured that by eye and with the cheap tape from my toolbox because these are the sorts of things that matter later.

The mirror was nailed to the mantel with old iron brads. I could hear the brads scrape faintly when I rocked the frame forward; the sound made me think of a hinge and a breath. I slid a putty knife under the bottom edge between the brads and eased the glass forward until the frame scraped the plaster. Behind it, folded flat against the wall, was a small diary: neat, narrow, the sort of book that had been written in with a very small, very steady hand.

I palmed the diary and felt the grain of its cover while the mirror returned to its place with a soft, rustling click. When I opened the book the handwriting ran on tight lines about angles and lamps and the way a slice of light would travel across the floor in March. I read one line aloud without meaning to: "Measure the angle at noon; do not trust the hour by the clock." The writing sat there like an instruction and a warning at once.

I wanted to check the floorboards because a house that keeps secrets often hides keys where a person might kneel to look for them. Two feet east of the hearth I found a plank that rode up under the heel when I stepped on it. A screwdriver pried the board loose and under it lay a small brass key, dull with age but warm from my hand the moment I picked it up.

There was a tapping then, very faint and regular, as if someone were turning a page behind the other side of the wall. It was not the settling that I’d expected; it had a rhythm — one-two, pause, one-two — and when I put my palm flat on the plaster I could feel the tiny modulation through the wood.

Back in front of the mantel I did a small experiment: I held my hand at a point I had marked on the sketch — seven inches left of center, at roughly the height of the mirror’s lower edge — and lifted it slowly. The reflection followed, but not perfectly. For a fraction of a second the glass showed my hand a beat after my hand had moved, as if the mirror were watching my gesture through a slow feed.

I closed the diary and let the brass key sit on top of it. The house hummed around me like an engine idling. I decided then to test the optics properly: precise measures, lamp angles, a repeatable note on where the lag happened. I made a note in the margin of the envelope and, as I packed the putty knife back into the toolbox, I felt the first, clean obligation of a problem I could solve.

## The draft

I had the match in my fingers because I had a habit of making ritual out of measurement — a small, deliberate flare I could control when everything else refused to be neat. The lamp had guttered while I was in the attic; the wick had gone faint and the hearth was cool when I came back down. I struck the match and brought it to the wick. The flame settled into the cone I'd measured earlier: six feet from the mantel, eighteen inches above the hearth, seven inches left of the mirror's centre. The attic slat cut the lamp's beam into a thin, pale line that fell straight to the seam.

I read the last page aloud because the diary had always been strict about saying things twice. The new entry I found tucked behind the others was dated March 25, 1972 and said, in Hannah's small, tight hand: "March 25, 1972: A leaving asks a taking; the seam will not be satisfied without an offered place." I read it exactly as written: "A leaving asks a taking; the seam will not be satisfied without an offered place."

The seam caught the light and the glass answered the way the diary promised — not with whim but with geometry. The shimmer concentrated like a held breath along the hairline; the reflected stair folded wrong again, and the blue cold in the mirror sharpened to an edge. For a second my hand and its reflection were two different clocks: mine a fraction ahead, hers a fraction late. Then the seam was a midplane and the world tightened around it.

I spoke her name because the paper told me to, because names with measures seemed to be the language this house understood. "Hannah Hale," I said, and then the line from March 24: "Speak her name and give the leaving."

Something moved in the glass not as an image but as a will. My reflection — my face, my hands — stopped matching mine and began to obey the other side. Where I lifted my hand she did not lift hers in time; instead she loosened her fingers and let them fall to her side, the small domestic motion of someone who was not astonished. The mirror's Hannah did not mouth 'light' this time; she inhaled, and the sound I heard was not from the room but from inside my own skull.

A pressure slid down my spine like a cord being pulled. I felt my center detach — not an ache, but the certainty of moving away from a place I had occupied. There was a flutter, a tilt in the lungs, and then I was looking at the parlor from the wrong side of everything: from behind the glass where the light was colder and the stair went the other way. My hands were pale, pressed to the inside of the mirror; they were me and not-me, reaching out across a surface that would not yield.

On the room-side my body — my hands, my coat, my face — moved without the insistence of my will. Mrs. Haverford, who had come up the path and was in the doorway with her knitting basket, gave a small, sensible sound — a gasp the way a sensible woman gasps when a kettle boils over. The woman in my body smiled, buttoned the cuff of my coat the way someone checking a sleeve does, and said, in my voice but not mine in intent, "Thank you, dear. I can walk now."

The logic of the diary and the light was a clean thing; it had not lied. The seam had wanted symmetry, a place offered to receive what it would let go. It asked for a taking and the house, obeying its angles, provided one.

I pressed my forehead to the cool, unhelpful glass and watched the only proof I had of a bargain keep to its terms: Hannah, alive with my body, turned toward the street and took a step. Behind the glass my breath fogged the reflected pane; beyond it a woman moved off the mat toward a life that had cost me mine.

I measured the six feet again because measuring was the part of this that felt like control, then I pencilled a small cross on the floor seven inches to the left of the mirror’s centre and taped a strip of envelope paper there to hold the mark.
